items.title: The name
items.text: Still Coca-Cola’s. In May 2019 it put New Coke, “the same recipe from 1985,” into 12-ounce cans sold in a bundle online and dispensed free from pop-up vending machines, to promote “Stranger Things.”[^25] It described this to investors as “a first-of-its-kind partnership with Netflix.”[^31] Mother Jones put the run at 50,000 cans; the company’s page gives no number.[^27]

items.title: The formula
items.text: Sold as Coke II until 2002 by two later accounts, or 2004 by the Associated Press.[^19][^21][^22] Coca-Cola says only that it “is no longer available in the United States.”[^1]

items.title: The old formula
items.text: Back as Coca-Cola Classic in July 1985 and the leading brand by 1990.[^6][^14] The word “Classic” came off US packaging from 2009; Canada had dropped it in 2007.[^19][^20]

items.title: The company
items.text: Net income rose from $629 million in 1984 to $934 million in 1986, and its share of the US market reached a record.[^4][^11]

items.title: The protest
items.text: Mother Jones reports that membership in Old Cola Drinkers of America fell by 90% after the old formula returned.[^27]

items.title: The lesson
items.text: Coca-Cola itself now publishes the episode under a headline about the most memorable marketing blunder ever, as “testimony to the power of taking intelligent risks.”[^1]

blocks.title: One owner, three names
blocks.subtitle: The formula was never sold. What changed was what Coca-Cola was willing to call it.

nodes.what: The new formula takes the name Coke and replaces the original.[^3]
The original returns as Coca-Cola Classic; the new formula stays on sale as Coke.[^6]
